title: The Eko, Dedication of Merit
speaker: Kakumyo Lowe-Charde
summary: Kakumyo Lowe-Charde's main teaching emphasizes the importance of embracing imperfection and uncertainty in meditation practice, encouraging individuals to let go of preconceptions and expectations in order to tap into a more expansive and receptive state. By cultivating mindfulness and attention to the subtle differences between imagination and experience, one can develop a more authentic and embodied practice that is guided by intuition rather than rational thinking. This approach allows for a deeper connection with the present moment, leading to greater ease, joy, and satisfaction in daily life.

So we're in the Soto Zen tradition, and ritual is an important part there.

Soto Zen teaches and demonstrates practice through the use of lots of different, very particular forms: ways that things are done, ways in which we set aside our habits and our preferences and just fall into accord, right?
If we can do that, we're taught by the forms.

These can be mundane things like putting your shoes straight when you take them off and you go inside, or saving the ends of vegetables to put in a stock, or folding a drying towel into thirds before you hang it up.
Those are all things that we do here, for instance.

It could be ceremonial things like how you turn or how you bow in the zendo, or more internal, esoteric things like the shape of the heart and the voice when you're making an invocation or a blessing or an offering.
So there's a variety of ways in which we're taught by a ritual in this way.
The eko at the end of the chant is one of those, in which we're invoking a certain kind of presence.
We're offering specific gratitude.
We're asking for specific benefit.
Well, specific gratitude, at least.
The benefit may be a little bit more amorphous, depending on your particular phrasing.
Often the benefit that is asked for is for others.
We're transferring the benefit that we may have accrued from these practices, from this attentiveness to our state of mind, to others.
And I would say that for a lot of people it's easy to skip over this.
It's easy to come into the practice with an idea of what I want, what I need, what I want to accomplish, how I want to benefit.

And also with a pocket full of deadlines, a list of competing priorities and limited resources, this felt pressure to make the Dharmic time count: I've got to be efficient in my harvesting of Dharmic goodness so that I can take care of the rest of life.
That's par for the course.
And it's also an example of a fractured state of mind, right?
It's a reactive self.
It's not who we really are, in a big way.

The sooner we can recognize those smaller, more dissonant states and tilt ourselves in the direction of the mind which is more wholesome, more integrated, more open, less suffering, the better off we are.
The tradition of merit is one of those practices that helps us catch that more easily, right?
That allows us to notice and defuse states of mind that are fractured, that are marked by grasping, fear, anxiety about self-interest.
Of course it happens at the end of a chant, but it can also happen many times during the day, right?
Hopefully our life is embedded in practice, and this intent to be of benefit, to not wreak havoc, cause suffering to ourselves, is something that is stable in life.
And we're making effort with some frequency throughout the day.
So every time we turn the mind in the direction of practice, turn the mind towards letting go or opening up, that's an opportunity.
Washing dishes, you can make a little offertory towards those who don't have clean water.
Or negotiating with a child, you can make a little offertory that someday they're going to appreciate this.
Or checking email: that all beings may realize their interconnectedness, whatever it may be.
They can be throwaway offertories.
You don't have to have something poetic and Zen-sounding and deep and profound.
It's just little markers.
It's just little reminders that my little vision, my autopilot of how isolated I am in life, is not the real picture.
There's more interconnection.
And it's just the frequency of those reminders that really counts.
You don't need a gong.
You just need a second or two, right?

One of the things that I find in talking about this with people, especially, I think, in convert Zen audiences in the West, is that we tend to be materialistic, scientifically sophisticated, psychologically astute.
And so a certain skepticism is pretty safe, right?
We like our causal interpretations of the world.
It goes in a little easier than a devotional one.
And we tend to define things in terms of meditation and how it impacts meditation, how it supports or expresses mindfulness.
I think, probably, there's a respect for other views.
But there can be a weariness of absorbing an interpretation which diminishes our sense of control, or a predictable causality.
And dedication of merit is not a predictable causality, right?
It really flies in the face of that.
It's taking the lines that are easy to draw and that are just drawn for us, and it's erasing them, right?
It's making them less clear, more ambiguous.
I think most people find that they do that naturally at certain times.
Those lines fall away when there's enough reminders, enough situational cues.
But for that to continue to inform us throughout life, we need to have lots of little reminders, lots of little practices that keep it at hand.
I think the way Soto Zen tends to talk about meditation supports this.
I would say, in contrast to many traditions, we're doing Shikantaza, right?
What is that?
How do you define that?
It emphasizes the mysterious, the subterranean, the imperceptible aspects of this practice.
It's not typically presented as effects and why, that more causal approach.
You get more of that in Theravada and Vajrayana approaches.
For us, meditation is really a manifestation of realization, right?
It's not a means of getting you closer to it.
And I think part of that is acknowledging just how limited our conceptual faculties are in this realm of non-duality.
We don't do a great job of representing that or expressing that.

I think it's also an acknowledgement that our internal alchemical transformation happens or starts happening long before we have the ability to put the mind somewhere and have it stay there, that we are adept at concentration.
We can feel the effects of practice long before we can feel like we're good at meditation, for the vast majority of people.
I think that's a wise approach.
Certainly, I come into this with a boatload of, I'm a little type A, productive and achievement oriented and busy.
So that shows up in practice.

If I'm trying to engineer it, if I'm trying to think my way through some of my practice works better, faster, more reliably, whatever, it's very hard not to cling to some idea of what it should look like, what it should feel like.
And I can get pretty sneaky about how I disguise that idea, but it's happening.
If I can release that causality, there's nowhere to hang that idea.
So I find it really helpful, really refreshing in that way.
It just feels like an important antidote for 21st century America.
The sooner we can divert some of that karmic momentum that wants to define and aim at something, to map, "this is how it'll go," the better.

So the Pali Canon, the early teachings of the Buddha, describes the first three fetters that disappear as the result of practice as being skeptical doubt, attachment to rites and rituals, and the belief in a separate self, an enduring self.
Two of those are laying out the ways in which we can miss on this front, right?
We can lean in the direction of skeptical doubt and end up with either a kind of cynicism or a kind of paralysis, a lack of confidence that we can do it, that we have access.
Or we can steer too far towards the attachment to our rites and rituals and get superstitious or passive or complacent about practice, about the internal work of it.
So I find keeping a sense of what those boundaries are helpful.
I can recognize when I'm starting to lean in one direction or the other.
I find that if I can stay in between those, avoid those particular misses, then having a practice of dedicating merit is clarifying of intention, right?
It's like this diagnostic that I run many times a day: where's the mind, and what matters to me right now?
It's a little like dreams being a symbol of what caught you in the day before.
I get to see some of that through what pops up in little dedications.
What's just taking up space in mind?
It also cultivates this relationship with a more expansive view.
It makes it easier for me to feel tangibly that my practice is witnessed, and I don't have to define who's witnessing it, but that there's a broader reception there.
And I feel like it cultivates a sensitivity to what may be needed, right?
Having to know what's needed, it's not that kind of cognitive thing, but a willingness to listen for what is sacred, what is at depth, what is symbolic.
When might a spontaneous micro ceremony be needed?
What might help me fall into alignment with this moment?
That's a pre-verbal language.
It's not loud.
And we need a tender heart.
I think that's the organ that is receptive to that language.
We tend to look for justification.
I tend to look for justification and rationale.
I don't know if you do.
I'm guessing you probably do.
I tend to look for justification for what I do, what I believe, and part of fluency with this nonverbal language of the heart is just having the space to listen.
I feel like that is another description of Shikantaza: to listen for what is appropriate, what is needed, what is beautiful, what is meaningful right now.
The more I can be open to that, the more I can be influenced by that, right?
The more my narrative of who I am and what I'm doing and what counts can get diverted.
And I feel like when I can pivot easily, when I can be surprised, when I have to change, when I can do that with grace and with ease, that's a sign that practice is going well.
That's one of my big ones.
So I want to have as many of those opportunities to test that as possible.
Yeah.
So I think the refinement there is a matter of doing meditation, those micro meditations during the day of just taking a breath and being open to what's next.
What really is needed right now?

It's easy to guess at the right answer.
We're very good at just making it up and filling in the blanks.
But the thing is, it has a different flavor.
It feels different.

Don't buy it.
Try again."
Try again.
